author: Ishita Jain
text:
Just wrapped up a project that pushed me to think like a Junior ML Engineer, not just a model-fitter.
The challenge: predict a gas turbine's energy yield (TEY) from live sensor data, in a way a hiring manager — or a service team relying on it at 2am — could actually trust.
Here's what that meant in practice:
🎯 Framed it as a real prediction problem, not just a regression exercise — defined the target, the units (MWh), and exactly who would use the output and why.
🚫 Built a leakage-free feature set. Two sensors (CO, NOx) correlated almost perfectly with the target — and I excluded both, because they're measured in the exhaust stack after combustion finishes, the same moment the turbine's output is already determined. Using them would mean training on information I wouldn't actually have at prediction time.
⏳ Validated honestly with a chronological split — trained on earlier years, held out the latest year untouched, and never reported a training score as if it were the real result.
📊 Compared a Linear Regression baseline against a Random Forest, and reported the improvement transparently — held-out MAE dropped from 2.90 MWh to 1.53 MWh, a ~47% reduction, backed by R² of 0.983.
🔍 Read the residuals, not just the headline metrics — found the model was heteroscedastic, quietly less certain and slightly under-predicting exactly at the highest turbine loads. Wrote that down as a documented limitation, not a flaw to hide.
🌡️ Stress-tested it against next summer's peak temperature. Push the model 7°C past its trained range, and typical error jumped from 1.5 MWh to 7.1 MWh — with zero warning from the model itself. That single result reshaped my monitoring plan: watch the input distribution before a bad prediction ever ships, not just the error after the fact.
📝 Closed it out with a full model card AND a plain-language explanation for a non-technical plant manager — because a model nobody can explain isn't one anybody should trust.
Result: 92/100, evaluator confidence 93%, certified by ProoV by Projectstudy.in

The biggest takeaway wasn't the R² score. It was learning that "the model is very accurate" is a claim — but "off by 1.5 MWh on held-out data, and here's exactly where it struggles" is evidence. That distinction is the whole job.

text:
I'm proud to share that I've officially graduated from University of Bristol with a First-Class Honours MEng in Engineering Mathematics.
A highlight was achieving a 75% in my Master's dissertation, exploring how modifying the training and evaluation of state-of-the-art recurrent and transformer-based deep learning models can improve the quality of wearable health data.

My research has also been accepted for publication and presentation at the ML4ITS (Machine Learning for Irregular Time Series) Workshop, held at the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (https://ecmlpkdd.org/2026/ 2026) 2026. I'll be presenting this September in Naples, Italy.

ML4ITS brings together researchers developing machine learning methods for irregular time series, with applications spanning healthcare, wearable sensing, industrial monitoring, mobility and energy systems. My work focused on reconstructing missing physiological data from Garmin smartwatches collected from a participant with epilepsy, improving data quality for downstream seizure risk forecasting. More broadly, it contributes to the growing use of consumer wearable devices for continuous, non-invasive health monitoring.

A huge thank you to my brilliant supervisors and co-authors Nawid Keshtmand, Jeff Clark, Roussel Desmond Nzoyem, and Amberly Brigden for their continued mentorship and support throughout this project.

I am actively looking for ML Engineer opportunities in the space. If you're attending the conference- or if your team is hiring- I'd love to connect.
And and final huge shoutout to my best mates and fellow engineers. I couldn't have asked for a better group of people to share the last four years with, and I'm really going to miss calling Bristol home!

Choosing the “right” programming language isn’t about trends — it’s about using the right tool for the job.

Here are 5 of the most in-demand languages in today’s market, along with where they shine (and where they don’t):

—

🐍 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Simple syntax, massive ecosystem, great for automation
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Data analysis, AI/ML, scripting, backend services
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Slower performance compared to compiled languages

—

☕ 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Platform independence, strong typing, enterprise stability
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Large-scale systems, banking, Android apps
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Verbose syntax, slower development cycles

—

🟨 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗦𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: Runs everywhere, huge ecosystem, full-stack capability
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Web apps, APIs, front-end + back-end (Node.js)
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Inconsistent behavior, dependency overload

—

⚙️ 𝗖++
🧰 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀: High performance, low-level memory control
📊 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Game engines, embedded systems, high-frequency trading
⚠️ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿: Steep learning curve, memory management complexity
